title: Jonah the Stoat and the Pumpkin Pile
markdown:
The Grand Academy Library was a temple of knowledge that smelled of polish and crushed leaf. Sunlight like liquid gold poured through stained glass — each pane a picture of greenery — onto floors so clean they reflected rumours. Wisdom slept on towering shelves, waiting for curious minds to prod it. This sacred place was also the kingdom of Jonah the stoat. His fur shone like a polished acorn. His whiskers twitched with sharp precision. He was the Academy’s Head Greenhouse Keeper, and his heart, solid as old oak roots, beat with quiet pride for his plants.

This season the air fizzed. The Annual Gardening Show had arrived, and Jonah’s prize winners were pumpkins: plump, glorious orbs, each glowing with harvest-moon light. He had whispered secrets to them on dewy mornings, sung to them, and defended them from chill. Now the royal spheres were destined for a place of honour inside the library itself.

Then Elara the shrew arrived, unnervingly neat, bows perfectly tied, mood a summer breeze that somehow always blew on Jonah’s nerves. Her voice tinkled like tiny bells. She did not brag. She simply appeared, plants unmarked, leaves unweary, as if kissed by sun and blessed by rain. Jonah, whose worries clung like wet soil, found her constant sunshiny politeness a personal weather event.

“Oh, Jonah,” she chirped. “Your pumpkins are simply… round. Such a satisfying shape.”

It was not an insult. Jonah’s mind filed it with every crooked leaf he had ever failed to straighten. He sighed a puff of dusty air and began to arrange his orbs with the care of a mapmaker who distrusted continents.

The library, usually still as a held breath, admitted a gust through a window left a finger too open. Loose pages of old gardening books — prickly vines, potions for reluctant soil — swirled around the pumpkins like startled moths. Jonah lunged for paper. He did not see the decorative marble gardener, a statue whose stony stare judged dust motes for living. The statue, lighter than dignity should allow, wobbled, teetered, and sat with a sorry thump in Jonah’s finest pumpkin. The dent was neat. The embarrassment was not.

“Oh dearie me,” Elara murmured, looking sweeter for the concern. “Perhaps a stronger stand? Something more solid?”

Jonah’s control slipped like a dropped stitch. He borrowed a trolley from the library’s book-moving system, a machine that had last been oiled when the Academy was a rumour. In his fluster he forgot the wheels were desert-dry. One snagged on a stray ivy vine that had no business indoors. The trolley lurched. Two prize pumpkins escaped, bumped across the polish, and kissed the sensible shoes of Professor Burrowell, a badger of impressive size and more impressive quiet, deep in a manuscript said to whisper of forgotten mushrooms.

The Professor huffed. A radiator that had slept for years woke with a hiss and a theatre’s worth of steam. Glasses became two confused moons in a fog. Jonah’s face supplied the sunrise.

Luca the lynx stood in the doorway, twilight fur, sunset eyes, Jonah’s younger sibling and the only creature in the building not auditioning for panic. He did not gasp at the pages or the dent. He walked as if the steam had invited him. One knowing nudge freed the trolley’s stubborn wheel. Then, with a rumble that settled the air, he began to stack pumpkins: one, two, a third, a neat tower in the exhibition’s heart. The steam made a curtain. The silliness behind it became, briefly, a show worth watching.

Jonah’s breath caught in his tiny throat. It was so simple it felt like cheating, and also like being rescued by the obvious. Elara’s polite vocabulary flew off like sparrows. For the first time since Jonah had known her, she was quiet. Professor Burrowell, not easily moved, gave a short approving nod over glasses that were remembering how to be glasses.

Jonah put his paws on the next pumpkin and set it where Luca pointed. The tower accepted the help without comment. His grin arrived late and sheepish, chasing the last of the worry. “All it needed was stacking.”

Luca’s smile could have thawed a January bed. He did not list Jonah’s wrong turns. He left room on the pyramid for the dented pumpkin, bruise turned to the back, still part of the harvest.

When the exhibition doors opened, the plain strong pile drew a steady stream of looks that Elara’s flawless petals had to share. Visitors circled. Someone asked if the dent was a variety. Jonah, who might once have fainted at the question, said it was a variety of afternoon. The radiator hissed like a gossip who had decided to stay for the party.

He stood beside the tower and bumped Luca’s shoulder, a thank-you too loud for words and too small for a speech. The dented pumpkin sat in the stack as if it had meant to be interesting. Jonah, who had wanted a flawless court of moons, found he preferred a tower that could take a knock and still hold — and a lynx who could see the forest, and the pile, when Jonah could see only the dent.
characters: Jonah (a stoat greenhouse caretaker), Luca (a lynx sibling)
